history.heading: Andean civilisations
paragraphs: Bolivia's high plateau, the Altiplano, was home to the Tiwanaku civilisation, which flourished near Lake Titicaca from around 500 to 1000 CE and built impressive stone monuments, including the Gateway of the Sun. The Aymara kingdoms followed, and in the 15th century the region became part of the Inca Empire.
The lowlands to the east were inhabited by many other peoples, including the Guaraní and the Moxos culture, which built raised fields and earthworks.

history.heading: Silver and Spanish rule
paragraphs: The Spanish conquered the area in the 1530s and called it Upper Peru. In 1545 enormous silver deposits were discovered at Cerro Rico in Potosí, which became one of the largest and richest cities in the world. Indigenous people were forced to work in the mines under the mita labour system, in which countless died.
Indigenous rebellions, such as that led by Túpac Katari in 1781, challenged colonial rule. Bolivia declared independence in 1825 and was named after Simón Bolívar.

history.heading: Instability and lost territory
paragraphs: The 19th and 20th centuries brought frequent coups and wars with neighbours. Bolivia lost its Pacific coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879–1884), land to Brazil, and much of the Gran Chaco to Paraguay in the Chaco War (1932–1935).
The 1952 National Revolution introduced universal suffrage, land reform and nationalisation of the tin mines. Military dictatorships followed from 1964 until democracy was restored in 1982.

history.heading: Plurinational state
paragraphs: In 2005 Evo Morales became the first president from the indigenous majority. His government nationalised gas, reduced poverty and adopted a new constitution in 2009 that renamed the country the Plurinational State of Bolivia. His attempt at a fourth term led to a disputed election and crisis in 2019.
His party, the Movement for Socialism (MAS), returned to power in 2020 but split bitterly. Amid an economic crisis, the 2025 elections ended nearly two decades of MAS government.

culture.heading: Indigenous heritage
paragraphs: Bolivia has one of the largest indigenous populations in the Americas, mainly Quechua and Aymara, along with dozens of smaller groups. The constitution recognises Spanish and 36 indigenous languages as official.
Catholicism blends with Andean traditions, such as offerings to Pachamama (Mother Earth). The Carnival of Oruro, with its devil dance (diablada), is recognised by UNESCO.

culture.heading: Life in the Andes
paragraphs: La Paz, the seat of government, sits around 3,600 metres above sea level, and the twin city of El Alto is even higher; a cable car network links them. Sucre is the constitutional capital. The Salar de Uyuni is the world's largest salt flat.
Popular foods include salteñas (baked pastries), api (a maize drink) and quinoa. Women in the Andes often wear the traditional pollera skirt and bowler hat. Football is the most popular sport.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Bolivia is a unitary presidential republic with a president elected for five years and a bicameral Plurinational Legislative Assembly. Indigenous rights, regional autonomy and natural resource ownership are central political themes.
Politics has been divided between the indigenous and rural highlands, long the base of MAS, and the more conservative eastern lowlands, centred on Santa Cruz.

politics.heading: Foreign relations
paragraphs: Bolivia continues to seek sovereign access to the Pacific Ocean, a long-standing issue with Chile; in 2018 the International Court of Justice ruled that Chile has no obligation to negotiate. Bolivia is in the process of becoming a full member of Mercosur.

economy.heading: Natural resources
paragraphs: Bolivia has rich natural resources, including natural gas, silver, zinc, tin and some of the world's largest lithium reserves, in the salt flats. Natural gas exports to Brazil and Argentina funded the boom of the 2000s and 2010s, but production has declined.
Agriculture is important in the lowlands, with soybeans and cattle, while much of the population works in the informal sector.

economy.heading: Recent crisis
paragraphs: Falling gas revenues, fuel subsidies and the depletion of foreign currency reserves led to an economic crisis in the 2020s, with fuel shortages, rising inflation and a black market for dollars. The currency is the boliviano. Despite this, poverty fell significantly over the previous two decades.
